ut.description: Ultrasonic testing in Newark, NJ: wall thickness surveys, corrosion checks and UT weld inspection at port, refinery and terminal sites. Request a quote today.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Gauging in Newark, New Jersey
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing in Newark, New Jersey: wall thickness surveys on piping, tanks and vessels, corrosion checks on steel structure, and angle-beam UT inspection of welds. Work is aimed at the container port, the petroleum and chemical terminals around Newark Bay and the Arthur Kill, and the fabrication shops and bridge owners nearby. Send the asset list and the governing code through the quote request form and a Level II technician's scope will come back for your review.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Newark

Newark sits inside the Port of New York and New Jersey, and the Port Newark–Elizabeth Marine Terminal is the largest part of that port. Every ship-to-shore container crane there is a welded steel structure that carries wind load, boom loads and thousands of lift cycles a year. Thickness readings on boom tubes, legs and sill beams, and angle-beam examination of repaired joints, are routine work for a crane owner trying to keep a terminal open.

A few miles south, the Linden and Elizabeth waterfront holds one of the largest concentrations of refining and petroleum storage on the East Coast. Piping, fractionation towers, drums, heat exchanger shells and aboveground tanks in that corridor all lose wall to corrosion, and UT is the standard way to measure how much. The same method serves the chemical and polymer plants that share the Arthur Kill, and the cold-storage, food and warehouse operations that have grown along the New Jersey Turnpike.

Away from the water, Newark has older industrial building stock, rail yards, bridges over the Passaic River and elevated roadway structure. Thickness surveys on corroded steel members and shear-wave checks on repair welds are common requests from the engineers who maintain these assets. Whatever the asset, the same questions come first: what is it made of, what is its nominal wall, and what code decides whether a reading is acceptable?

What ultrasonic testing finds, and what it cannot

An ultrasonic probe sends a sound pulse into the part and times the echoes that return. For thickness gauging, the delay between the front surface and the back wall gives the remaining wall. For weld work, a probe on an angled wedge sends shear waves through the weld volume and the technician watches for echoes from reflectors such as lack of fusion, cracks and slag. Unlike surface methods, UT reports on the inside of the metal, which is why it is the method of choice for corrosion under insulation checks once the jacketing is opened at a test point and for the root of a thick groove weld.

UT has limits that a good scope states up front. Heavy pitting scatters the sound and can produce a reading that looks plausible but is wrong. Rough, scaled or painted surfaces weaken coupling to the probe. Coarse-grained castings and some austenitic welds attenuate the beam. Very thin wall under about one-eighth inch needs special probes. And a straight thickness reading says nothing about a crack that runs parallel to the surface, which is a reason to pair UT with surface methods when a component has a cracking history. For that, our Newark magnetic particle page and penetrant page explain the companion examinations.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Newark work

Which document governs a UT job depends on what the asset is. Process piping at a Linden or Elizabeth plant is normally built and maintained to ASME B31.3, with examination methods in paragraph 344 and acceptance in Table 341.3.2. Pressure vessels follow ASME Section VIII, where Division 1 Appendix 12 covers ultrasonic examination of welds. Structural steel for buildings and cranes is usually welded under AWS D1.1, whose Clause 8 includes UT of groove welds and its own acceptance classes. Steel highway and rail bridges fall under AWS D1.5.

The test procedure itself is written to ASME Section V. Article 4 covers weld examination, Article 5 covers UT of materials, and Article 23 carries SE-797, the practice for contact thickness measurement. For plain wall-loss surveys, our guide to Article 5 thickness requirements explains what a defensible procedure must state. Inspection plans for in-service equipment follow the owner's API 510, API 570 or API 653 program. Under those programs the owner's authorized inspector is responsible; Atlantis performs the NDE and reports the thickness and indication data to that inspector.

New Jersey adds its own regime. The Bureau of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Compliance in the state Department of Labor and Workforce Development regulates boilers, pressure vessels and refrigeration systems, issues inspection certificates, and has done so since 1913. An owner-user may run an in-house inspection organization under N.J.A.C. 12:90-3.19. Our New Jersey inspection services hub collects the state-level context in one place.

How ultrasonic thickness testing is performed

On corroded steel, the working tool is a dual-element probe, which has separate transmit and receive crystals angled slightly toward each other. It copes with rough surfaces and pitting far better than a single-element contact probe. Before readings start, the technician calibrates on a step block made of the same material and covering the expected thickness range, then verifies against a known thickness at intervals during the job. An A-scan display stays on the instrument so that a doubled back-wall echo on thin wall, or a laminar split, is recognized rather than recorded as a number.

Readings are taken at the condition monitoring locations the owner has defined, usually marked on an isometric or a vessel sketch. On a pipe elbow the technician grids the extrados, where wall loss concentrates; on a tank shell, courses are measured at set heights. Where the surface is hot, the work needs a high-temperature probe, a couplant rated for the temperature and a correction for how sound speed changes with heat. Insulated lines mean the owner opens a window in the jacketing or has a rigger remove a section before the probe can reach the steel.

For weld examination, the technician builds a reference level from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, selects a 45, 60 or 70 degree shear-wave probe suited to the thickness, and scans both sides of the weld where access allows. Indications are sized against the reference, located by beam path and probe position, and compared with the acceptance table in the governing code. Scanning a weld on a fabricated crane boom or a thick process line takes methodical overlap, and the technician records the extent of scan along with any area that could not be reached.

Who performs the work

Atlantis has no office in Newark. Technicians are mobilized to your site, whether that is a terminal, a plant or a fab shop, for the agreed scope. They are qualified under the company's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up the instrument, performs the examination and interprets the results. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. The Level III responsible for review is Anoop Rayavarapu, who holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

If you need to see how that framework is built before you award work, we can walk you through the written practice and the procedure approval flow. Owners writing their own program can start with written practice development or look at outside Level III consulting. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

What the UT report contains

A useful UT report lets a reviewer reproduce the job from the paper. Each report names the component or line number, the drawing or isometric reference, the procedure and its revision, the code and acceptance table applied, the instrument, probe and couplant used, the calibration block and its identification, and the technician with qualification level. Thickness surveys add a grid or table of readings by location with the nominal and minimum required wall, plus the lowest reading highlighted. Weld examinations add the probe angle, scan plan, reference level, scanning gain, and every recordable indication with length, depth and amplitude relative to the reference.

Each indication is dispositioned as acceptable or rejectable against the named criteria, and any area not scanned is stated. Sketches show where each reading or indication sits on the component. Findings go to the owner's authorized inspector or engineer, who decides what the numbers mean for remaining life and next inspection date. Atlantis reports data and does not make the fitness-for-service decision.

Planning a UT job in Newark

Port and terminal sites in Newark run on security rules. Expect credential checks before you reach a berth, safety orientation, and work permits for hot or confined areas. Plant work in Linden and Elizabeth adds site-specific hazard training and, in process areas, gas monitoring. List the people who need access early so the paperwork does not slow the start.

Weather shapes the schedule. January and February bring cold that stiffens couplant and chills instruments; a low-temperature gel, or warming the instrument between readings, usually fixes it. In July and August, steel in sunlight can run hot enough to need a high-temperature setup. Coastal humidity and salt air speed up surface corrosion, so freshly cleaned test points may need re-cleaning after a delay. Turnaround and outage seasons at the refineries concentrate demand in spring and fall, which is a good reason to share your scope early.

Access matters as much as weather. Crane booms, tank roofs and elevated pipe racks need scaffold, a lift or rope-access support from the owner or a contractor. Traffic on the Turnpike and the port's truck gates affects how equipment and people arrive, so build travel buffers into your plan. Because crews travel to site, a clear scope with line numbers or asset IDs avoids lost days.

UT versus MT and PT for your Newark job

Pick the method by the question you are asking. If the concern is wall loss or buried weld flaws, UT is the right tool. If the concern is a surface crack in a ferromagnetic weld, such as a lifting lug or crane pin boss, magnetic particle testing is faster and more sensitive at the surface. If the part is stainless, aluminum or a nonferrous fitting, liquid penetrant testing covers surface-breaking cracks that MT cannot. Many Newark jobs combine two methods on the same weld, for example MT of the cap and UT of the volume.

Our national pages explain each method in more depth: ultrasonic testing, the ultimate UT guide, and the MT versus PT comparison.

Training your own UT technicians

Some Newark owners prefer to build an in-house team. Atlantis teaches theory and practice for the employer to use under its own written practice: see UT Level 1, UT Level 2, and the wider ultrasonic testing training page, or practise on the UT simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A it is the employer who certifies the people who pass. For eligibility questions start at SNT-TC-1A eligibility, and for local options see NDT training in Newark.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic testing cover in Newark, NJ?
faq.a: In Newark we perform thickness surveys on piping, vessels, tanks and structural steel, plus angle-beam UT of welds in refinery, terminal, crane and fabrication work. The scope is set by the code, the drawing and the owner.

faq.q: Can you measure wall thickness on crane booms and port structures?
faq.a: Yes. Boom tubes, legs and sill members can be gauged with a dual-element probe, provided the owner arranges safe access and the surface is cleaned at each test point. Readings are logged by location against nominal wall.

faq.q: Which code applies to UT of piping welds at a Linden-area plant?
faq.a: Process piping is usually governed by ASME B31.3, which points to ASME Section V for method and Table 341.3.2 for acceptance. The owner or its engineer may add stricter limits, and the report names exactly which table was used.

faq.q: Does ultrasonic testing replace radiography on welds?
faq.a: Only where the construction code and the owner allow it. Some codes permit UT of production welds, and AWS D1.1 has its own UT criteria. The substitution is agreed with the owner, engineer and authorized inspector before work starts.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Newark?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, so the quote should state the location, access arrangements and any badging the site requires. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Who is the inspector of record on API 510, 570 or 653 equipment?
faq.a: The owner’s authorized inspector. Atlantis performs the examination and delivers thickness grids and indication data to that inspector, who judges remaining life and sets the next inspection date.

faq.q: Can UT be done on hot piping or insulated lines?
faq.a: Hot surfaces need a high-temperature probe and couplant, and a correction for sound speed. Insulated lines need the owner to open a window in the jacketing first. We confirm both points when scoping the job.

faq.q: What information should I send to get a UT quote for a Newark site?
faq.a: Send the asset or line list, nominal wall, material, operating temperature, the governing code, access details and target dates. Add earlier thickness data if you have it so readings can be compared against a baseline.

faq.q: Can you train our own technicians in ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis teaches UT theory and practice for employers building a program under SNT-TC-1A. The employer certifies its own personnel, so completion of a course is one input to that certification and not a certificate by itself.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Newark, NJ | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Newark, NJ: yoke and wet-method MT of welds, lugs, crane steel and pressure parts at port and plant sites. Quote on request.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Newark, New Jersey
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out magnetic particle inspection in Newark, New Jersey, on welds, lifting lugs, pins, crane structure and pressure-part attachments made of carbon or low-alloy steel. Mag particle testing is a fast surface check that shows cracks a visual inspection can miss. If your site is in the port, the refinery corridor or a fabrication shop, describe the parts and the code in the MT quote request and we will return a scope for review.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Newark

Newark's economy is built on moving things. The Port Newark–Elizabeth Marine Terminal handles most of the containers and a large share of the vehicles that enter the Port of New York and New Jersey, and the equipment that does the lifting is steel under repeated load. Spreader attachment points, trolley rail welds, wheel and pin boss welds, twist-lock hardware and the corner castings that tie containers to chassis are all magnetic steel and all classic MT candidates.

Along the Arthur Kill and Newark Bay the work shifts toward process equipment. Weld repairs on pressure vessel shells, nozzle-to-shell welds, support lugs on towers, structural tie-ins on pipe racks and tank shell-to-bottom welds get MT after grinding or after a repair weld cools. Tank farms add a steady stream of requests for floor and shell weld surface checks during outages.

Elsewhere in the city, steel fabricators, rail equipment shops and bridge owners use the method on structural welds. Repairs to steel members on elevated roadway and rail structures often call for MT of the repair weld before the member returns to service. Wherever it is applied, MT answers the same blunt question: is there a crack open to the surface or just under it?

What MT finds, and what it misses

The method depends on magnetism. A magnetic field is induced in the part, and where a crack interrupts the field, a small leakage field forms at the break. Fine iron particles, dusted on dry or carried in a liquid bath, collect at that leakage and outline the crack. The result is immediate and easy to read, and the technician can see length and orientation at once.

Because it relies on magnetic flux, MT works only on ferromagnetic material. Carbon steel and low-alloy steel respond well. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper alloys and most nickel alloys do not, and a Newark site that mixes stainless piping with carbon steel structure needs both MT and a second method. Our Newark penetrant testing page covers that nonmagnetic side. MT also detects only surface and slightly subsurface flaws; it does not size depth and cannot find buried lack of fusion, which is where ultrasonic testing in Newark comes in.

Surface condition matters. Heavy scale, thick paint, weld spatter and oil all reduce sensitivity, and a coating thicker than the procedure allows can hide a fine crack. The technician checks the surface first and asks the owner to clean or strip where needed.

Codes and acceptance criteria that apply

For MT the method requirements come from ASME Section V, Article 7, with the construction code supplying acceptance limits. Pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1 use Appendix 6 for MT methods and acceptance. Process piping under ASME B31.3 relies on paragraph 344.3 for the method and Table 341.3.2 for the limits. Structural steel under AWS D1.1 and bridge steel under AWS D1.5 carry their own visual and surface-examination requirements. ASTM E709 is the guide to the method and ASTM E1444 is the standard practice.

A short explanation of the Article's rules is in our guide to Article 7 magnetic particle requirements. For general background read the complete MT guide.

New Jersey's Bureau of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Compliance, part of the state labor department, regulates pressure equipment in the state and expects repairs to be documented by the rules it enforces. Owner-users with in-house programs operate under N.J.A.C. 12:90-3.19. For the wider state picture see our New Jersey inspection hub. Under API 510, 570 and 653 programs the owner's authorized inspector is accountable; Atlantis performs the MT and supplies the findings.

How magnetic particle inspection is done

The most common field tool is the electromagnetic yoke, which clamps two legs on the part and drives flux between them. Yokes are portable, and the technician repeats the examination with the legs turned roughly ninety degrees so that cracks lying in any direction are caught. Before use the yoke is proved with a lifting-force check: an AC yoke must lift a defined weight at the pole spacing in use, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke must lift considerably more. Where the part is large or an overall field is wanted, prods or a cable wrap may be specified instead.

Particles come in two main forms. Dry powder in visible colors suits rough weld surfaces outdoors; wet particles in a carrier suit smoother surfaces and give finer sensitivity. Fluorescent wet particles are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area, which makes tight cracks glow. Colored contrast paint on the surface may be used under visible particles to improve contrast. The technician follows a written procedure for field strength, dwell time, particle application and viewing conditions.

After the examination, parts that will be welded, machined, painted or put into service near sensitive instruments may need demagnetizing to remove residual field. A field indicator or gauss meter confirms the residual level before the part is released. Cleaning removes particles so later coatings adhere.

Who performs the work

There is no Atlantis office in Newark, so a Level II technician is mobilized to your location for each job. Technicians are qualified under the company's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians set up the equipment, perform the MT and interpret it. An ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Our founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

If your own written practice needs work, see written practice development, or talk to us about Level III consulting. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

What the MT report contains

A complete MT report identifies the component, drawing or weld number, the procedure and its revision, and the code and acceptance table. It lists the method used (yoke, prods, wet or dry, visible or fluorescent), the particle product and batch, the equipment and its calibration or lift-test status, the field direction and surface condition, and the technician and level. Each indication is recorded with location, length and orientation, and marked on a sketch or photograph. Every indication is dispositioned against the acceptance criteria named in the contract, and the report states whether the part was demagnetized.

The report is reviewed and signed before it is released. We hand the data to the owner or engineer who decides on repair, re-test or release.

Planning a Newark MT job

Winter is the main constraint here. Wet particle baths and contrast paints are formulated for a working range, and very cold steel can slow particle mobility or make the carrier thicken. The procedure sets the range, and a technician may warm the part or switch products when Newark cold falls below it. Summer heat is the opposite problem: hot steel dries a wet bath too fast and can dull fluorescence.

Fluorescent work needs darkness, which is awkward outdoors in a terminal in daytime. A portable shroud, a tent or a night shift on the owner's side usually solves it. On the port and in plants, expect badging, orientation and work permits. Rail and truck traffic at gates affects when crews can enter.

Refinery and tank-farm outages concentrate MT demand in spring and fall, so early scoping helps. Provide access, a clean test surface, and power if prods or a bench unit are specified.

MT versus PT and UT in Newark

Choose MT when the part is magnetic and the concern is a surface or near-surface crack: welds on crane steel, pins, lugs and vessel attachments. Choose penetrant testing when the part is stainless, aluminum or any nonmagnetic alloy, or when the surface is too rough for particles. Choose ultrasonic testing when the concern is wall loss or a flaw below the surface. Our MT versus PT comparison sets out the trade-offs, and the national MT page covers the method in more depth.

Training your own MT technicians

For owners who want in-house capability, we teach MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 under the wider magnetic particle testing training program. Employers certify under SNT-TC-1A; our courses supply the theory and practice. See NDT training in Newark and practice tests for exam preparation.

faq.q: What parts can you inspect with magnetic particle testing in Newark?
faq.a: Welds, lugs, pins, crane and equipment steel, vessel attachments and structural members made of carbon or low-alloy steel. Parts must be ferromagnetic and the surface must be clean enough for particles to move.

faq.q: Does MT work on stainless steel pipe or aluminum fittings?
faq.a: No. Austenitic stainless steel and aluminum are not magnetic, so particles will not outline cracks. Liquid penetrant testing is the usual surface method for those materials in Newark plants and shops.

faq.q: Which standard governs MT of welds on pressure vessels?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 7 sets the method, and ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 gives MT methods and acceptance for vessels. Piping under B31.3 uses its own paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2.

faq.q: Do you use fluorescent particles outdoors at port sites?
faq.a: Fluorescent MT needs a darkened area and UV-A light, so outdoors we use shrouds or tents when the procedure calls for it. Visible dry or wet particles are the alternative for bright locations.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or lab in Newark?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope. Please send the location, access rules and any badging requirements with your quote request and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Is demagnetizing included after MT?
faq.a: It is done when the procedure or the owner requires it, for example before welding, machining or coating. A gauss or field-indicator check confirms the residual field, and the report records the result.

faq.q: How does cold weather in Newark affect magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Procedures set a working temperature range for particles and carriers. In a hard winter we warm the part, change product or use dry particles, and record the surface temperature in the report.

faq.q: What do I need to send for an MT quote?
faq.a: Send the part list or weld map, material, surface condition and coating, governing code and acceptance table, access arrangements and target dates. A photograph of a typical weld helps us plan technique and equipment.

faq.q: Can you train our technicians in MT?
faq.a: Yes. We offer MT Level 1 and Level 2 training for employers that certify under SNT-TC-1A. The employer certifies its own people, and our training supplies the theory and hands-on practice.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye Penetrant | Newark, NJ
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Newark, NJ: dye penetrant inspection of welds, stainless and aluminum parts, valves and fittings. Send details for a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) and Dye Penetrant Inspection in Newark, New Jersey
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT provides liquid penetrant testing in Newark, New Jersey. Dye penetrant inspection reveals cracks and pores that are open to the surface on welds, castings, forgings, valve bodies and machined parts, in steel and in nonmagnetic alloys alike. We mobilize a technician to your site, run the examination to the written procedure and report each finding against the code. Start with the PT quote request.

Where penetrant testing is used in Newark

Newark's shipping and processing economy handles a wide mix of metals. Chemical and polymer plants along the Arthur Kill run stainless steel and nickel alloy piping, heat exchanger tube sheets and reactor nozzles that MT cannot examine. Penetrant is the usual surface method on those welds, particularly after repair or modification.

Port equipment uses aluminum and stainless in places that matter, including hydraulic fittings, stainless handrails and hardware, and cargo-handling components made of nonferrous alloys. Food and cold-storage operations clustered near the Turnpike work with stainless process piping and tanks that are welded and polished in place, where a cracked weld becomes a sanitation as well as a structural issue.

Fabrication shops and machine shops in Essex and Union counties add castings, forged flanges and machined parts that need a final check before shipping. For all of these, PT is the standard surface test whenever the material is not suitable for magnetic particles.

What penetrant testing finds and what it misses

The method works by capillary action. A low-viscosity liquid is applied to a clean surface and given time to enter any opening. The excess is removed, a developer is applied, and the developer draws the trapped liquid back out so that a crack shows as a bright or colored line against the background. The principle is simple and the sensitivity is high on fine tight cracks, which is why it is trusted on critical parts.

The same principle limits it. A discontinuity must be open to the surface, so PT cannot find buried flaws, lack of fusion below the surface, or wall loss. Smeared metal from grinding or peening can close a crack and hide it, which is why etching or careful cleaning matters. Porous materials absorb penetrant and produce a confusing background. Heavy paint, oil or scale blocks entry altogether.

When a part must be checked for both surface cracks and internal flaws, the surface step is PT and the volume step is UT. For ferromagnetic material, MT in Newark is often faster. The related UT page for Newark covers wall and weld volume.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V Article 6 defines the liquid penetrant method. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 gives PT methods and acceptance for pressure vessels. Process piping under ASME B31.3 specifies PT in paragraph 344.4 with limits from Table 341.3.2. For general industry, ASTM E165 is the standard practice, and structural and bridge steel under AWS D1.1 and D1.5 refer to the applicable visual and surface requirements for the weld in question. Our explainer on Article 6 penetrant requirements goes through the rules, and the national penetrant page covers the method in general.

Materials used on nickel alloys, stainless steel and titanium are often required to be low in sulfur and halogens, so contamination does not cause cracking later. The procedure names the penetrant family and the contaminant limits, and the technician records batch numbers.

In New Jersey the Bureau of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Compliance in the state labor department oversees pressure equipment. Repairs to boilers and vessels are documented under its rules, and PT records form part of that file. See the New Jersey inspection services page for the state context. For plants running API programs, the owner's authorized inspector stays responsible and Atlantis reports PT findings to that person.

How dye penetrant inspection is performed

The job starts with cleaning. Weld spatter, paint, oil and corrosion product are removed mechanically or with a solvent, and the surface is dried. Penetrants are classed by type and method: Type II visible dye penetrants are red and viewed in white light, while Type I fluorescent penetrants are viewed under UV-A in a darkened area. Methods differ in how the excess is removed: solvent-removable, water-washable or post-emulsifiable. Solvent-removable visible dye is the common field choice because it works anywhere with no water supply.

The penetrant stays on the surface for a dwell time set by the procedure, often five to thirty minutes depending on material and flaw type. The excess is wiped away carefully, because over-cleaning can pull penetrant out of a real crack. Developer, usually a fine white powder suspended in solvent, is sprayed on in a thin even film, and the technician examines the surface after the developing time in adequate light. Indications are measured and recorded, then the part is cleaned.

The temperature of the part and the materials matters. Standard procedures cover a working window of roughly cool to warm room conditions; below or above it, the technician must demonstrate that the penetrant still performs, usually on a comparator block. A comparator with known cracks verifies the process on the day.

Who performs the work

Atlantis has no staffed location in Newark. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope and work under the company's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians perform and interpret the examination. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Our founder Anoop Rayavarapu holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

Owners who need a program of their own can start with written practice development or Level III consulting.

What the PT report contains

The report names the component, weld or drawing number, the procedure and revision, the code and acceptance criteria, the penetrant type and method, and the product manufacturer and batch numbers for penetrant, cleaner and developer. It records surface and ambient temperature, dwell and developer times, the lighting or UV intensity for fluorescent work, and the comparator check. Each indication is described by type (linear or rounded), location and size, marked on a sketch, and dispositioned as acceptable or rejectable.

The technician, qualification level and date appear on the form, and a Level III review is noted where the contract requires it. The owner or its engineer then decides on repair and re-examination.

Planning a PT job in Newark

Temperature is the main planning point. In Newark winters, steel in an exposed yard can sit well below freezing, and penetrant and developer become sluggish. The options are to warm the part, use a product qualified for lower temperature, or wait for the weather; guessing is not one of them. In summer, sun-heated steel dries solvent too quickly and can flash off penetrant before it enters a crack, so shade or cooling is needed.

Humidity and rain affect developer and cleanliness, and salt air from the harbor leaves residue that must be cleaned. Fluorescent PT needs a dark enclosure, so plan for a booth or tent. Port and plant access follows normal rules: credentials, safety orientation and permits. Where confined space is involved, solvent vapors need ventilation and gas monitoring.

Give us access to the weld or area, a clean surface and a stated sequence if PT must follow grinding or precede a coating. Early scoping around outages helps.

PT versus MT and UT in Newark

PT is the tool when the metal is not magnetic or when you need the most sensitive surface check on a clean weld. Magnetic particle testing is faster on carbon steel and can find slightly subsurface flaws. Ultrasonic testing is the choice for wall loss and internal weld flaws. The MT versus PT comparison helps you decide.

Training your own PT technicians

If you want your own penetrant technicians, we run PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 within the penetrant testing training program, plus the PT simulator for practice. The employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A. Look at NDT training in Newark for local detail and practice tests to prepare.

faq.q: What does liquid penetrant testing find in Newark industrial work?
faq.a: Surface-breaking cracks, laps, pores and seams on welds, castings, forgings and machined parts. It works on steel, stainless, aluminum and other nonporous metals, but it cannot see flaws that do not reach the surface.

faq.q: When should I choose PT instead of MT?
faq.a: Choose PT when the material is not magnetic, such as stainless steel or aluminum, or when the surface is too rough for particles. MT is usually faster on carbon steel and also catches slightly subsurface flaws.

faq.q: Which standards cover dye penetrant inspection of vessels and piping?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 for the method, Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for vessel acceptance, and B31.3 paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2 for piping. ASTM E165 is the general industry practice.

faq.q: Can PT be done in freezing weather in Newark?
faq.a: Only if the procedure is qualified for the temperature. Otherwise we warm the part, use a suitable product or reschedule, and record the surface temperature in the report so the result is defensible.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a lab or office in Newark?
faq.a: No. A technician is mobilized to your site for the agreed scope. Send the location and access rules with your enquiry and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Do you control sulfur and chloride on stainless and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Yes. When the specification requires low-contaminant products, we use materials that meet it and record the manufacturer and batch numbers so you can show they were controlled.

faq.q: What preparation do I need to do before PT?
faq.a: The surface must be free of paint, oil, scale and spatter, and dry. If grinding or peening was done, mention it, because smeared metal can hide cracks and may need to be etched or removed.

faq.q: What do I send to get a PT quote for a Newark site?
faq.a: Send the parts or weld list, material, size, surface condition, governing code and acceptance criteria, location and access details. Photographs of a typical weld help us choose the penetrant system and plan lighting.

faq.q: Can you train our own technicians in PT?
faq.a: Yes. We offer PT Level 1 and Level 2 training for employers who qualify personnel under SNT-TC-1A. The employer certifies its own people; our course provides the theory and practice.
